mainTopic: Returning to חבר status, judging one's own animals, and how blemished holy animals are sold
overview: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about people who took on the strict practices of a חבר and then dropped them. רבי מאיר says they are never accepted back. רבי יהודה makes it depend on private versus public, and an איכא דאמרי gives another version of that split. רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה say they are always accepted, and רבי יוחנן rules like them. A second ברייתא says that at first a חבר who became a גבאי could never return, but later the rule changed so that once he quits he is like anyone else. A story follows about רב הונא בר חייא, where רב יוסף and רבה each act on a different line of that ברייתא. Next comes a ברייתא that a person may not inspect his own בכור, though he may rule on his own קדשים, מעשר and טהרות. The גמרא explains that the ban applies to a יחיד מומחה, and that in the other cases he has no real reason to lie. The chapter then ends, and a new משנה teaches that פסולי המוקדשין are sold in the market and weighed by the litra, while בכור and מעשר are not.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: Those who left are never taken back
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי מאיר: anyone who took on the practices of a חבר and then dropped them can never be accepted again.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: All those who went back on their commitment are never accepted again. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a ברייתא about people who left the status of חבר. The first opinion, from רבי מאיר, is the strictest: once you leave, you can never come back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is talking about an עם הארץ who committed to the strict practices of a חבר and then abandoned them. רבי מאיר holds that the trust is broken for good, so the word עולמית, meaning 'ever', closes the door completely. This sets up the range of opinions that follow.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Rabbis taught', the opening words of a ברייתא
Someone trusted to keep the laws of purity and tithes carefully
They went back on their commitment

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
And all of them who went back on their commitment,
phrases.notes: 'All of them' are the people discussed just before on the daf, who took on the practices of a חבר.

phrases.english: they are never accepted again,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the ברייתא about returning to חבר status.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, a person who leaves the practices of a חבר is never accepted back.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: It depends whether they left in private or in public
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says that someone who dropped the practices secretly is not accepted back, but someone who dropped them openly is.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: If they went back on it in private, they are not accepted. If they did it in public, they are accepted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with רבי מאיר and divides the case in two. What matters to him is how the person left.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person who quietly stopped the practices while still acting like a חבר in public was being two-faced, so he cannot be trusted again. A person who left openly was honest about it, so if he wants to return, we believe him.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't flip it around. In this version, leaving in public is the better case, because the person was honest. Leaving in secret is the worse case.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
If they went back on it in private,
they are not accepted;
if in public, they are accepted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי מאיר by splitting the case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who left in secret is not accepted back, and someone who left in public is accepted back.

steps.title: A second version: It depends how they kept the practices at first
steps.stepSummary: Some report רבי יהודה's view differently: the question is whether they kept the practices even in private at the start, or only in public.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: If they did their practices even in private, they are accepted. If they did them only in public, they are not accepted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports another version of the private/public split. Now the question looks at how sincerely the person kept the practices back when he was a חבר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the test is the person's original sincerity, not the way he left. If he kept the practices even when no one was watching, he was truly committed, so he may return. If he kept them only for show, his return cannot be trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: 'There are those who say', introducing another version

phrases.english: There are those who say:
If they did their practices in private,
phrases.notes: This means back when they first became a חבר, they kept the practices even when no one was watching.

phrases.english: they are accepted;
if only in public, they are not accepted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אִם עָשׂוּ דִּבְרֵיהֶן בְּמַטְמוֹנִיּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of the private/public split from step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who kept the practices even in private may return. Someone who kept them only in public may not.

steps.title: רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה: Always accepted
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה say that in every case the person is accepted back, based on the פסוק 'Return, wayward children'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה say: Either way they are accepted, because it says: 'Return, you wayward children.'
steps.whatsHappening: Two more תנאים give the most lenient view: anyone who wants to return is accepted, no matter how he left. They support this with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה, they do not look at how the person left or how sincere he was before. The פסוק shows that the door for returning is always open. This is the opposite end from רבי מאיר.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה אוֹמְרִים:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha say:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין כָּךְ וּבֵין כָּךְ מְקַבְּלִין אוֹתָן,
phrases.english: Either way, they are accepted,
phrases.notes: 'Either way' means whether they left in private or in public.

phrases.english: because it says:
"Return, you wayward children."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה אוֹמְרִים: בֵּין כָּךְ וּבֵין כָּךְ מְקַבְּלִין אוֹתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with all the earlier views and takes the most lenient position.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Anyone who returns is accepted back, no matter how he left.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן rules like the lenient pair
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק of כפר עכו reports that רבי יוחנן ruled like רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק of the village of עכו said in the name of רבי יוחנן: The הלכה follows that pair.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling on the argument: the הלכה follows the lenient pair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'That pair' means רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה. So in practice, a person who left the practices of a חבר is always accepted back when he returns.

keyTerms.meaning: A man from the village of עכו

steps.whatToRemember: There are four views in a row: רבי מאיר (never accepted), רבי יהודה (depends on private versus public), the איכא דאמרי version, and רבי שמעון with רבי יהושע בן קרחה (always accepted). The הלכה follows the last pair: always accepted.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק אִישׁ כְּפַר עַכּוֹ
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak of the village of Akko said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
The law follows that pair.
phrases.notes: 'That pair' is רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה from the step just before.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument in favor of step 4.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Someone who left the practices of a חבר is always accepted back when he returns.

steps.title: The early rule: A חבר who became a tax collector is removed for good
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא says that at first, a חבר who became a גבאי lost his status, and even if he quit the job he was not taken back.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: At first they used to say: A חבר who became a tax collector is pushed out of his חבר status. If he quits, he is still not accepted back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא on a related case: a חבר who becomes a גבאי. It first gives the older, stricter rule, and this sets up the change that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking the job of a גבאי costs a person his status as a חבר. Under the early rule, the damage was permanent: quitting the job did not let him come back.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
At first they used to say:
A חבר who became a tax collector,
they push him out of his חבר status;
if he quit, he is still not accepted back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא on a related case: a חבר who became a tax collector.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Under the early rule, a חבר who became a tax collector lost his status permanently, even after quitting.

steps.title: The later rule: Once he quits, he is like anyone else
steps.stepSummary: Later the Sages changed the rule: a tax collector who quits is like any other person and can be accepted as a חבר again.
steps.simpleTranslation: Later they changed their minds and said: If he quit, he is like any other person.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with the later, more lenient rule that replaced the early one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The former גבאי is no longer stuck with a permanent stain. Once he leaves the job, he is treated like any regular person who wants to become a חבר, so he can be accepted again.

keyTerms.meaning: They changed their minds and said

steps.whatToRemember: For a חבר who became a tax collector, the final rule is the later one: once he quits the job, he can be accepted back like anyone else.

phrases.english: They changed their minds and said:
If he quit, he is like any other person.

steps.triggerLanguage: חָזְרוּ לוֹמַר: פֵּירַשׁ — הֲרֵי הוּא כְּכׇל אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the early rule of step 6 with a more lenient one.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A former tax collector who quits is treated like anyone else and can become a חבר again.

steps.title: The story of רב הונא בר חייא becoming a tax collector
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים honored רב הונא בר חייא, but dropped him when he became a גבאי. He said he had quit. רבה went back to him, but רב יוסף did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once the חכמים needed רב הונא בר חייא. רבה, רב יוסף and 400 pairs of scholars went up to him, and he set out 400 chairs for them. Later they heard he had become a tax collector, and they sent him a message: 'Go to your important job, go back to what you were before.' He answered: 'I have quit.' רב יוסף did not go back to him, but רבה did.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real-life story that tests the rule from the last two steps: can a חבר who became a tax collector be taken back once he quits?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story sets up a split. רב הונא בר חייא says he quit, which is exactly the case in the ברייתא. רבה and רב יוסף then act differently, and the next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: Tax collector. Such a person was suspected of being dishonest.
I have taken it back, I have quit

phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya —
one time, they needed him

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה עָיֵיל גַּבֵּיהּ רַבָּה וְרַב יוֹסֵף
phrases.english: Rabba and Rav Yosef went up to him
along with four hundred pairs of Sages.
He heard that they were coming,
so he tied together four hundred chairs for them.
Later they heard that he had become a tax collector.
They sent him a message:
Go to your important position,
go back to your former state.
He sent back to them: I have quit.
Rav Yosef did not go to him;
Rabba went.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִיָּיא אִיצְטְרִיכָא לֵיהּ שַׁעְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the rule from Steps 6-7 in a real case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After a חבר who became a גבאי quit, רבה accepted him back and רב יוסף did not.

steps.title: רב יוסף and רבה explain why they acted differently
steps.stepSummary: Each one points to a different part of the ברייתא. רב יוסף relies on the early rule (not accepted). רבה relies on the later rule (like any person).
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: We learned that if he quit, he is not accepted. רבה said: We learned that the חכמים changed their minds and said that if he quit, he is like any other person.
steps.whatsHappening: Each אמורא explains his behavior in the story by quoting a different line of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף follows the first ruling: even after quitting, he is not taken back. רבה follows the later ruling ('חזרו לומר'), which accepts him like anyone else. Since the later ruling is the one that stands, רבה's approach matches the final word of the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: He quit, he stepped away from the job
They changed their minds and said

steps.whatToRemember: A tax collector who quits can be accepted again as a חבר. That was the later ruling, and רבה acted on it.
steps.confusionAlert: רב יוסף and רבה are quoting the same ברייתא. It is not two different sources. רב יוסף quotes its first ruling, and רבה quotes the later one.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: We learned:
if he quit, he is not accepted.
phrases.notes: This is the earlier ruling from Step 6.

phrases.english: Rabba said: We learned:
they went back and said:
if he quit, he is like any other person.
phrases.notes: This is the later ruling from Step 7.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר: תְּנֵינָא, פֵּירַשׁ — אֵין מְקַבְּלִין אוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the different actions in the story of Step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יוסף relies on the early ruling and rejects him. רבה relies on the later ruling and accepts him.

steps.title: A ברייתא on inspecting one's own animals
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא says anyone may inspect firstborn animals except his own. But he may inspect his own קדשים and מעשר, and he may decide about his own טהרות.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A person may inspect all firstborn animals for blemishes, except his own. He may inspect his own consecrated animals and his own tithe animals. He may also be asked about, and rule on, his own pure foods.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ברייתא about when a person may decide questions that affect his own property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a בכור, the owner gains if he finds a blemish, because then he may eat it. So he may not inspect his own. With his own קדשים, מעשר and טהרות, the ברייתא trusts him even though he also has a personal interest.

keyTerms.meaning: Firstborn animals. They may be eaten only if they get a blemish.
His foods that are kept ritually pure

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A person may inspect all firstborn animals
except for his own,
and he may inspect his own consecrated animals,
and his own tithe animals,
and he may be asked about his own pure foods.
phrases.notes: He may decide for himself whether his own food stayed pure.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כׇּל הַבְּכוֹרוֹת אָדָם רוֹאֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person may not inspect his own בכור, but he may inspect his own קדשים and מעשר and rule on his own טהרות.

steps.title: What case is the ברייתא talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case 'except his own' means. It cannot mean one person alone, because one person is not trusted to permit a בכור anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: A person may inspect all firstborns except his own. What case are we dealing with? If you say one person inspecting alone, is he even trusted?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the first line of the ברייתא and asks what situation it describes. It rules out the first option right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא meant a single inspector, it would not need to single out his own animal. One person alone cannot permit any בכור. So the ברייתא must mean something else, and this sets up the next move.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with?

phrases.english: The Master said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַבְּכוֹרוֹת אָדָם רוֹאֶה חוּץ מִשֶּׁל עַצְמוֹ
phrases.english: A person may inspect all firstborns except his own.
What case are we dealing with?
If you say it means one person,
is he trusted?
phrases.notes: The question assumes one person alone can't permit a בכור at all, so his own animal would be no different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes the first line of the ברייתא from Step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does 'except his own' refer to a single inspector or to one of three judges?

steps.title: With three judges, why suspect him?
steps.stepSummary: If the case is three judges, there should be no suspicion. A משנה says a judge who sat on the court for a woman's מיאון or חליצה may marry her, because he was only part of a court.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the case is three judges. But are they suspected? Didn't we learn: if a woman did מיאון or חליצה in front of him, he may marry her, because he is a court?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the second option, three judges, and then challenges it with a משנה that does not suspect a judge who sits on a court of three.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה about מיאון and חליצה shows that a judge who is part of a court of three is not suspected of acting for his own benefit. If so, why may a person not be one of three judges for his own בכור? The next step answers this.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't we learn in a משנה?
She did מיאון: a girl married off as a minor refuses the marriage
She did חליצה, the ceremony that releases a widow from יבום

steps.confusionAlert: The judge here is not suspected because he is only one of three judges. That is the whole point of the challenge.

phrases.english: Rather, it means one of three judges —
but are they suspected?
But didn't we learn in a mishna:
if she did refusal or ḥalitza before him,
he may marry her,
because he is a court!
phrases.notes: He was just one of three judges, so we don't suspect him of ruling for his own benefit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After ruling out one inspector, the גמרא tries three judges and challenges that option.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the ברייתא means one of three judges inspecting his own בכור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה in יבמות does not suspect a judge on a court of three, so there should be no reason to stop the owner from being one of the three.

steps.title: The case is one expert judge ruling alone
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about a single expert, a יחיד מומחה, who may permit a בכור alone. So he cannot permit his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the case is one judge. As רב חסדא said in the name of רבי יוחנן, a single expert can rule. Here too, it means a single expert.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem from steps 11 and 12. 'Except his own' is about one judge who is an expert.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 11 the גמרא said one person cannot permit a בכור. In step 12 it said three judges would not be suspected. The answer is a middle case: a יחיד מומחה is allowed to rule alone. Because he stands alone and benefits from the ruling, he may not decide about his own בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually. It opens an answer that keeps the first idea.
A single expert who is allowed to rule alone

steps.confusionAlert: Step 11 rejected the idea of 'one person' because an ordinary single person cannot permit a בכור. Now the גמרא says it does mean one person, but a special one: an expert. These two statements do not contradict each other.

phrases.english: Actually, it is about one judge,

phrases.aramaic: וְכִדְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: and it is like what Rav Chisda said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
by a single expert,
phrases.notes: רבי יוחנן said this about releasing vows: one expert can do it without a court of three.

phrases.english: here too it is about a single expert.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem raised in steps 11 and 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the case as a middle option: one expert judge
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Except his own' had to mean either an ordinary single person, who cannot permit a בכור at all, or three judges, who are not suspected
steps.terutzMaskana: It means a יחיד מומחה. He may permit a בכור alone, so he is suspected when the animal is his own.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows why the ban on judging your own בכור applies to an expert who rules alone and not to a full court.

steps.title: Why he may inspect his own sanctified animals
steps.stepSummary: He may rule on his own קדשים because he could have asked a חכם to cancel the dedication anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: He may inspect his own sanctified animals, because if he wanted, he could ask to be released from his vow about them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains the last part of the ברייתא. It starts with why a person may check his own קדשים for a blemish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person usually gains if his animal is found blemished. Here, though, he has an easier way out: he can ask a חכם to undo the vow that made the animal holy. Since he has no need to lie, he can be trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: Animals set aside as holy for offerings
To ask a חכם to cancel a vow

phrases.english: And he may inspect his own sanctified animals,
because if he wants, he can ask to be released from them.
phrases.notes: He could go to a חכם and undo the vow that made the animal holy, so he gains nothing by lying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to explain the next clause of the ברייתא from step 10
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person may inspect his own קדשים, because he could have had the dedication cancelled anyway.

steps.title: Why he may rule on his own tithe animals
steps.stepSummary: He may rule on his own מעשר animals because he could have blemished his whole herd before tithing.
steps.simpleTranslation: He may rule on his own tithe animals, because if he wanted, he could put a blemish on his whole herd.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the next clause of the ברייתא: why a person may judge his own מעשר בהמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he wanted his tithe animals to be blemished, he could have blemished the whole herd before separating the tithe. Since he had an easy and allowed way to get that result, he has no reason to lie about a blemish.

keyTerms.meaning: The tenth animal of the herd, which is set aside as holy
A blemish that makes an animal unfit to be an offering
Literally 'throw'. Here it means to put or inflict.

phrases.english: And his tithe animals,
because if he wants, he can put a blemish
phrases.notes: He would do this before separating the tithe, while the animals are not yet holy.

phrases.english: on his whole herd.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַעְשְׂרוֹתָיו, דְּאִי בָּעֵי שָׁדֵי בֵּיהּ מוּמָא בְּכוּלֵּיהּ עֶדְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same 'he could have done it anyway' reasoning as step 14
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person may rule on his own מעשר animals, because he could have blemished the whole herd before tithing.

steps.title: Why he may decide about his own pure foods
steps.stepSummary: He may decide about his own טהרות because even impure food is still useful to him when he is impure.
steps.simpleTranslation: He may be asked about his own pure foods, because the food is still fit for him to eat during his days of impurity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the last clause of the ברייתא: why a person may decide whether his own food became impure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the food is ruled impure, he does not lose it. He can still eat it at a time when he himself is impure. With so little at stake, he is not suspected of lying.

keyTerms.meaning: Foods kept in a state of ritual purity
Literally 'is asked'. Here it means he may decide the question himself.
The days when he himself is impure

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's rule: a person may not rule on his own בכור, because a יחיד מומחה ruling alone gains from it. He may rule on his own קדשים, מעשר, and טהרות, because in each case he has no real reason to lie. He could undo the vow, blemish the herd beforehand, or still eat the food.

phrases.english: And he may be asked about his own pure foods,
since they are fit for him during his days of impurity.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנִשְׁאָל עַל טׇהֳרוֹתָיו, דְּהָא חֲזוּ לֵיהּ בִּימֵי טוּמְאָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes explaining the three allowed cases from the ברייתא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person may decide about his own טהרות, because even impure food is still usable for him when he is impure.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A person is barred from judging only where he truly gains from the ruling.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter עד כמה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the chapter עד כמה ישראל חייבין with the traditional הדרן line.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'Until when are Israelites obligated.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is not an argument. It is the closing line that marks the end of the chapter עד כמה ישראל חייבין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The discussion of a חכם ruling on his own בכור, קדשים, מעשר and טהרות ends here. The next line begins a brand-new chapter with a new topic.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We will return to you': the phrase said when finishing a chapter
Name of the chapter being closed: 'Until when'

phrases.english: We will return to you,
'Until when are Israelites obligated.'
phrases.notes: That is the chapter's name, taken from its first words.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ עַד כַּמָּה יִשְׂרָאֵל חַיָּיבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter whose last topic (steps 10-16) was a person ruling on his own items.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The chapter עד כמה is complete.

steps.title: Blemished holy animals are sold like regular meat
steps.stepSummary: The new chapter's משנה rules that פסולי המוקדשין, whose money goes to הקדש, are sold and slaughtered in the butchers' market and weighed by the pound.
steps.simpleTranslation: All holy animals that became unfit for a קרבן: the profit from them goes to הקדש. So they are sold in the butchers' market, slaughtered in the butchers' market, and their meat is weighed by the litra.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter opens with a משנה. It sets the basic rule for how redeemed, blemished holy animals may be sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally we do not treat holy animals like plain market meat. But here the money goes to הקדש, so we allow full market treatment to get the highest price and protect הקדש from loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Holy animals that got a blemish, became unfit for a קרבן, and were redeemed
A litra, a unit of weight used to sell meat

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the base rule of the whole new chapter. Everything after it is an exception or a detail of it.

phrases.english: MISHNA: All disqualified consecrated animals,
phrases.notes: These are holy animals that got a blemish and were redeemed, so they are no longer brought as a קרבן.

phrases.english: the profit from them goes to the Temple treasury,
are sold in the butchers' market,
and are slaughtered in the butchers' market,
and are weighed by the litra,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new chapter after the הדרן line.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פסולי המוקדשין may be sold, slaughtered and weighed in the market like regular meat, because their profit goes to הקדש.

steps.title: Firstborn and tithe animals are the exception
steps.stepSummary: The משנה excludes בכור and מעשר from market treatment, because their profit goes to the owner, unlike other פסולי המוקדשין whose profit goes to הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Except for the בכור and the מעשר, because their profit goes to the owners. But with other disqualified holy animals, the profit goes to הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now gives an exception to the rule it just stated. It names בכור and מעשר and explains why they are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason for market treatment was to protect הקדש's money. With בכור and מעשר, the money goes to the owner (the כהן for a בכור), so that reason does not apply, and we do not treat holy meat like plain meat just to raise a private person's price. The משנה repeats the rule for other פסולי המוקדשין to show the contrast clearly.

keyTerms.meaning: A firstborn kosher animal, given to a כהן
The animal tithe, every tenth animal of the herd

steps.confusionAlert: בכור and מעשר are still holy animals with a blemish. The משנה is not saying they are outside that category. It only says they get a different selling rule because the money goes to the owner.

phrases.english: except for the firstborn and the animal tithe,
because the profit from them goes to the owners.
Disqualified consecrated animals: their profit goes to the Temple treasury.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the general rule of step 18 by naming an exception and giving its reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בכור and מעשר are not sold, slaughtered or weighed in the market, because their profit goes to the owner, not to הקדש.

steps.title: Weighing one portion against another for a firstborn
steps.stepSummary: Even though בכור meat is not weighed by the litra, the משנה allows weighing one portion of it against one portion of other meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one may weigh one portion against one portion with a בכור.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a small detail about בכור meat. A certain kind of weighing is still allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Weighing with standard weights by the litra is how regular meat is sold, so that is not allowed for a בכור. But putting a piece of בכור meat against a piece of other meat is not the normal market way, so it is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: A portion (here, a piece of meat of a set amount)

steps.whatToRemember: פסולי המוקדשין are sold in the market and weighed by the litra, because the money goes to הקדש. בכור and מעשר are not, because the money goes to the owner. But a portion of בכור meat may be weighed against a portion of other meat.

phrases.english: And one may weigh one portion against one portion with a firstborn.
phrases.notes: He means putting a piece of other meat on one side of the scale and בכור meat on the other, not using regular weights.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a permitted way of weighing בכור meat after step 19 excluded it from regular market weighing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may weigh a portion of בכור meat against a portion of other meat, since that is not the normal market way of weighing.
